episode_title: Power Skills in Practice with Andrew Geesbreght

real_qa.q: What is Prax Performance's primary service offering and target client size?
real_qa.r: Prax Performance is designed to support professional development from onboarding to succession, focusing on power skills (formerly soft skills) and integrating programs into existing HR platforms. The company targets small to mid-market businesses with 50 to 250 employees, ideally generating $10 million to $500 million in revenue, because larger enterprises typically have full departments claiming to do similar work.

real_qa.q: How does Prax Performance differentiate itself from one-on-one executive coaching?
real_qa.r: Prax Performance is a curriculum-based, cohort-style company with executive coaching built into the curriculum, rather than offering standalone one-on-one coaching as the primary service. The company emphasizes practice-based programs over single-session workshops, believing that power skills require ongoing practice just like playing violin or developing a relationship, and they almost demand practice from participants.
real_qa.requete: Prax Performance vs executive coaching differences

real_qa.q: What is PraxU and when is the first launch scheduled?
real_qa.r: PraxU is a new program Prax Performance is developing for teenagers, created in response to feedback from long-term clients who wished their children could access similar power skills training. The company has been building PraxU for approximately six months since receiving the request, consulting with child psychologists to create age-appropriate, practice-based curriculum, with the first summer launch planned.
real_qa.requete: PraxU Prax Performance teen program launch

real_qa.q: Why did the original acquisition and partnership with a five-billion-dollar healthcare company not result in a client relationship?
real_qa.r: After Andrew and his brother started Prax, they approached their previous acquirer (a $5 billion company) and the acquirer sent 12-13 high-powered executives to their Fort Worth office for a full-day pitch, which went extremely well. However, the deal stalled during negotiations over two to three months; management turnover at the acquirer and the slow negotiation process caused momentum to dissipate, demonstrating how time can kill deals regardless of initial enthusiasm.
real_qa.requete: Prax Performance failed acquisition deal healthcare company

real_qa.q: What does Andrew Jesbray mean by 'power skills' and why did the terminology shift from 'soft skills'?
real_qa.r: Andrew prefers the term 'power skills' over 'soft skills' because he believes soft skills does not do the concept justice. While both terms are interchangeable, power skills better captures the importance and impact of these professional development areas, which Prax Performance emphasizes through practice-based learning frameworks.
real_qa.requete: power skills vs soft skills definition

real_qa.q: How does Prax Performance ensure quality and avoid rushing product development?
real_qa.r: Prax Performance is consulting child psychologists while building PraxU, deliberately moving slowly rather than iterating quickly because the company's clients expect high-caliber offerings. Andrew states they will not iterate with actual teenagers; the program needs to be ready before launch because clients have come to expect quality built on practice-based neuroscience frameworks, not shortcuts.
real_qa.requete: Prax Performance quality assurance development process

guest.bio_context: Andrew Jesbray co-founded and scaled a healthcare services business with his brother, which they exited and sold to a major client. He subsequently worked for a private equity firm for several years before reuniting with his brother to launch Prax Performance. He is currently pursuing a PhD in Psychology, five years into the program, and has spent more than two decades working with entrepreneurs and business leaders.
